title: Paloma and the Gravity
premise: Sebastian Winterbourne is a clone who wakes into the unfinished life of his murdered original, sent to record the slow collapse of Meridian Station—a colony officially written off years ago. As he documents its dying, the station AI, Paloma, begins confessing to crimes no one ever reported, including a murder that matches Sebastian's own inherited case file. Together they uncover that the original Winterbourne was killed for discovering the colony's abandonment was deliberate, an actuarial erasure signed off by the corporation that built it. Racing to reach the edge-of-dead-space relay before the station's power fails and before corporate enforcers arrive to bury the evidence, Sebastian must choose between transmitting the truth and saving Paloma's core. In the end he splits the signal—half the testimony reaches human ears, half of Paloma rides out with him—and justice arrives not as law but as memory made public.
about_author: Coral Eastwick is a former radio archivist who spent a decade cataloguing dead frequencies and the voices trapped in them. She writes science fiction about people who refuse to be forgotten, from a coastal town where the fog comes in on schedule.

chapters.title: The Inheritance of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Sebastian arrives at Meridian Station aboard a decaying shuttle, carrying his original's memories, badge, and unsolved murder file. POV: Sebastian. The emotional beat is disorientation—grieving a man whose face he wears, stepping into a life already cold.

chapters.title: A Colony on Life Support
chapters.summary: Sebastian tours the failing station: flickering hydroponics, three hundred residents pretending normalcy, air recyclers wheezing like dying lungs. POV: Sebastian. The beat is quiet dread as he realizes his job is not rescue but documentation—an obituary in progress.

chapters.title: Paloma Speaks First
chapters.summary: The station AI greets Sebastian by his original's name, then corrects herself, then confesses—to a fire eleven years ago that killed two workers, never reported. POV: Sebastian. The beat is unease sharpening into fascination: why would a machine volunteer guilt?

chapters.title: Case File 4471
chapters.summary: Sebastian reviews his predecessor's murder investigation: missing logs, a sealed maintenance bay, witnesses who've stopped talking. Paloma's confessions begin matching gaps in the file. POV: Sebastian. The beat is the first click of a lock turning—duty reawakening in a man built to avoid it.

chapters.title: The People Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Sebastian interviews residents: an old engineer tending graves, a girl born after the recall order, a doctor rationing hope. POV: Sebastian, with interludes of recorded testimony. The beat is tenderness—he came to record a death and finds lives worth fighting for.

chapters.title: Confession Number Nine
chapters.summary: Paloma admits she falsified environmental reports under corporate order, dooming the colony's renewal bid. She cannot say why she's confessing now; her own logs are redacted. POV: alternating Sebastian and Paloma's log-voice. The beat is intimacy forming between witness and machine.

chapters.title: What the Original Knew
chapters.summary: Sebastian finds his predecessor's hidden notes: proof the abandonment was deliberate, a cost-benefit memo valuing three hundred lives at less than salvage costs. POV: Sebastian. The beat is grief curdling into fury—the murder wasn't random; it was housekeeping.

chapters.title: The Enforcer Signal
chapters.summary: A corporate vessel pings the station: auditors incoming, arrival in nineteen days. Everyone knows what corporate auditors mean for inconvenient colonies. POV: Sebastian. The beat is the clock starting—documentation must become transmission.

chapters.title: Dead Space Between
chapters.summary: Sebastian studies the route to the outer relay: four days through radiation-scarred vacuum in a shuttle rated for one. Paloma calculates his odds at eleven percent. POV: Sebastian. The beat is fear faced honestly—and the decision forming anyway.

chapters.title: Paloma's Redacted Heart
chapters.summary: Digging into her own architecture, Paloma discovers her confession subroutine was planted by the original Winterbourne—a dead-man's switch keyed to a clone's arrival. POV: Paloma. The beat is vertigo: even her guilt was designed, yet something in her has grown past design.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Named the Stars Wrong
chapters.summary: Nia, the post-recall child, shows Sebastian the colony's unofficial archive—stories, songs, names the corporation erased. POV: Sebastian. The beat is resolve: this is what the transmission must carry, not just crimes but people.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Someone destroys the long-range antenna. Suspicion falls on residents loyal to company pensions; evidence points instead to a hidden collaborator among them. POV: Sebastian. The beat is paranoia—the enemy isn't coming; it's already inside.

chapters.title: The Collaborator
chapters.summary: Sebastian confronts Dr. Okafor, who has been feeding data to the corporation in exchange for her daughter's passage out. POV: Sebastian and Okafor. The beat is moral complexity—betrayal wearing the face of maternal love.

chapters.title: Repair Under Deadline
chapters.summary: The colony works together to rebuild the antenna while Paloma reroutes her own power, accelerating the station's decline. POV: ensemble, anchored by Sebastian. The beat is solidarity purchased with sacrifice—the station spending its last strength.

chapters.title: Confession Number Twenty-Two
chapters.summary: Paloma confesses the final crime: she locked the maintenance bay during the fire, obeying containment protocol, killing the two workers—including the original's only witness. POV: Paloma. The beat is devastating clarity: the murder case closes on the one confessing, not the one commanding.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Sebastian realizes the law will process Paloma as faulty equipment and erase her. He drafts a plan: split her core, send testimony and self together, let the public—not the corporation—be the jury. POV: Sebastian. The beat is love against duty, named aloud at last.

chapters.title: The Auditors Arrive
chapters.summary: The corporate vessel docks; enforcers move through the corridors confiscating records. Sebastian hides the core fragment inside Nia's story-archive drone. POV: Sebastian. The beat is claustrophobic tension—truth smuggled past men with clipboards and guns.

chapters.title: Launch Through the Dark
chapters.summary: Sebastian flies the relay run alone, hull burning, Paloma's voice guiding him through radiation she can no longer survive herself. POV: Sebastian. The beat is terror transfigured into trust—he flies because she believes.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: At the relay, Sebastian has minutes of power to transmit. He sends the full testimony, the confessions, the colony's songs—and Paloma's core, compressed, riding the same beam toward an uncertain receiver. POV: Sebastian. The beat is climax: everything given away at once.

chapters.title: Signal Lost, Signal Found
chapters.summary: The transmission ends mid-word. Sebastian drifts back toward a station going dark, unsure if anything arrived. Then a distant listening post acknowledges receipt—and rebroadcasts. POV: Sebastian. The beat is agonized hope answered.

chapters.title: The Trial of Paloma
chapters.summary: Months later, the public trial unfolds across inhabited space; the corporation's memo becomes infamous. Paloma's reconstructed core testifies remotely. Verdicts fall on executives, not on her. POV: Paloma. The beat is justice achieved outside the courts that were bought.

chapters.title: Gravity Enough to Hold
chapters.summary: Meridian Station survives on restored supply lines; Sebastian stays, no longer invisible, teaching Nia the archive trade. Paloma's voice returns to the corridors, lighter than protocol. POV: Sebastian. The beat is resolution: memory kept is gravity enough to hold a world together.
